title: Lemon Mousse
subtitle: Whipped cream folded with lemon and beaten egg whites, set lightly in the fridge
excerpt: A light, airy mousse built from lemon juice, whipped cream, and stiff egg whites. No cooking required, chills for 2 hours and serves as a bright finish to any meal.
sourceNotes: Lemon mousse has been a fixture of British dinner-party cooking since at least the 1960s. The no-cook version, built on the natural thickening effect of lemon acid on cream, lightened with egg whites, is a common approach in British recipe books from Elizabeth David onwards.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to a day ahead and keep covered in the fridge. The mousse firms slightly on day two.

content.text: Lemon mousse is a cold, no-cook dessert, whipped cream sharpened with fresh lemon juice and zest, then lightened by folding through stiffly beaten egg whites. The contrast between the rich cream and the clean, sharp lemon makes it considerably lighter than it looks. The folding step is the one that matters: too aggressive and you knock out the air; too timid and you get white streaks. Fold in three stages with a large metal spoon and stop as soon as the mixture is uniform.

items.prepNote: for a more stable set, see method

content.text: In a large bowl, whip the double cream to soft peaks. Add half the caster sugar, the lemon juice, and the lemon zest, and fold gently to combine. The cream will thicken slightly as the lemon juice reacts with it. Set aside.

If you want a mousse that holds its shape for longer or needs to travel, soak the 2 gelatine sheets in cold water for 5 minutes. Squeeze out excess water and dissolve in 2 tablespoons of warm water in a small bowl. Leave to cool for 5 minutes, then drizzle into the whipped cream mixture, stirring quickly to distribute before it sets.
In a clean, dry bowl, whisk the egg whites to soft peaks. Add the remaining caster sugar and whisk to firm, glossy peaks, the whites should hold their shape but not be dry or grainy.

Scoop one large spoonful of egg white into the cream and stir to loosen. Add the remaining egg white in two stages, folding with a large metal spoon in slow, deliberate strokes, cut down through the centre, then sweep around and up. Fold only until no white streaks remain. Spoon into glasses or ramekins and refrigerate for at least 2 hours before serving.

items.cause: The egg whites were over-folded, knocking out the air, or the cream was over-whipped before folding.
items.fix: Whip the cream to soft peaks only, it should just hold its shape. Fold the egg whites in three stages and stop as soon as the mixture is uniform.

items.symptom: Mousse has separated by the time of serving
items.cause: The unstabilised mousse can weep if left for more than a few hours.
items.fix: Use the optional gelatine for advance preparation. Without gelatine, serve within 4 hours of making.
Reduce the lemon juice to 3 tablespoons and add an extra tablespoon of caster sugar. Taste the cream mixture before folding in the egg whites.

content.text: Best eaten the same day. With the optional gelatine, keeps well for up to 24 hours covered in the fridge. Do not freeze.
